title: False Consensus Effect
description: People overestimate the degree to which others agree with their opinions, beliefs, and behaviors.

sections.title: What It Is
sections.content: People overestimate the degree to which others agree with their opinions, beliefs, and behaviors.

sections.title: How It Actually Appears
content: A person who loves horror movies assumes everyone does and plans a group outing without checking.
A manager believes his decision is “obviously” the right one and is stunned when the team resists.
A smoker overestimates the percentage of people who smoke, thinking it’s more normal than it is.

sections.title: Common Behaviors
content: Saying “Everyone thinks this” when only a small subgroup does.
Believing that your values are universal.

sections.title: Warning Signs
content: You rarely encounter disagreement within your circle.
You feel genuine shock when poll results differ from your views.
You’ve never asked certain questions because you assumed the answer.

sections.title: Why It Works
sections.content: Our social environment is often filtered (we surround ourselves with similar people), and it’s easier to process the world as if others are like us. Ross, Greene, & House (1977) first demonstrated the effect, showing that people overestimate the percentage of others who share their choices.

sections.title: Protection Strategy
content: Before assuming consensus, ask a simple question: “What do you think?”
Expose yourself to diverse viewpoints intentionally.
When you think “everyone knows this,” test it on someone outside your bubble.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
content: Using the false consensus as an argument (“Everyone thinks so, so it must be right”).
Over-correcting and assuming you’re always an outlier.

sections.title: Real Scenario
sections.content: A product team designs a feature based on the assumption that “users love dark mode.” They push it aggressively without research. Launch reveals only 30% of users use it, and others find it hard to read. The team had projected their own preference.

sections.title: Key Insight
sections.content: “Everyone” is usually just the echo of your own voice. Check the room before you speak for the crowd.
